:::{#exm-sparse-vector}
#### A $2$-sparse vector

Take $\vx = \tp{(0, 3, 0, 0, -1)} \in \reals^5$.
It has two nonzero entries,
$x_2 = 3$ and $x_5 = -1$,
so it is [$2$-sparse](#def-sparse-vector).
It is also $3$-sparse, $4$-sparse and $5$-sparse,
since "at most $k$" allows fewer.
It is not $1$-sparse, because two of its entries are nonzero.
@fig-sparse-vector draws each entry as a stem from zero.

:::{#fig-sparse-vector}

```{r}
#| label: sparse-vector-plot
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Stem plot of the five entries of the vector (0, 3, 0, 0, -1) against
#|   their positions 1 to 5. Only position 2, with a stem up to 3, and
#|   position 5, with a stem down to -1, leave the horizontal zero line; the
#|   other three entries sit on it.
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5
values <- c(0, 3, 0, 0, -1)
entries <- tibble::tibble(position = 1:5, value = values)

entries |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = position, y = value) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    mapping = ggplot2::aes(xend = position, yend = 0)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "entry position", y = "entry value")
```

The entries of $\tp{(0, 3, 0, 0, -1)}$.
Only two stems leave zero, so the vector is $2$-sparse.
:::
